doc.title: Tony Marino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 25, 2025

title: Where to stand and where the time comes from
summary: He likes standing in the middle and takes time from the drummer's ride hand, adjusting to each drummer and Hal Galper's big beat.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That’s why the Delaware Water Gap gig there was right up your alley.
Do you have a spot on stage that you usually like to stand? I know some – I’ve heard bass players saying, “Well I want to be on your hi-hat side” or something like that.

Yeah a lot of guys are that way. I like to be in the middle for sure, between whatever the chordal instrument is and the drums, and I don’t have to be on the hi-hat side. When I’m locking in my time, I’m listening to what the right hand or – not everybody is a right handed drummer – but the time. Where the quarter note is coming from if we’re playing swing and jazz. You know? I want to know – that’s where I get the time from, his hands,

more than that hi-hat two and four. You know. So I’m listening for that. And that lets me know if I’m in sync with his quarter note, if I’m a little behind I’m a little bit – and every drummer’s different. You know I play with guys that really are on top of the beat and you’ve really gotta push. And then you get used to playing with a guy like that, then you’re playing with someone that plays a little behind the beat and you’re pushing him and you don’t want to push him. You know? You want to relax and breathe. You know I played – I noticed that playing with some tenor players and I was pushing them. I must have been playing with Lieb and it was, you know, fast. And I had to step back and say no I’m pushing him. You know? You’ve got a big space for every beat you know. Galper talked about that too, Hal Galper, when I play with him about the big beat. That was his whole thing, the big beat you know. So you know there’s a lot of room in that big beat. So you’ve got a guy that’s playing, I mean you don’t want to drag the tempo either but you have to – you’ve got to leave space for a guy like that. You know? That’s the way he plays. You know I don’t want to crush him.
